title: Classify three gas samples
question: Three sealed samples contain (A) only O₂ molecules, (B) only CO₂ molecules, and (C) O₂ and CO₂ molecules together without reacting. Classify each as an element, compound or mixture, and explain your reasoning. Assume each sample contains only the particles described.
hints: Count the different elements in each kind of particle. A molecule can contain atoms of just one element.
Ask whether different elements are chemically bonded in a fixed ratio, or whether separate substances are simply present together.
workedExplanation: A is an element: every atom is oxygen. O₂ molecules contain two atoms, but both are the same element.
B is a compound: carbon and oxygen atoms are chemically bonded in the fixed ratio 1:2 in CO₂.
C is a mixture: O₂ and CO₂ remain separate substances. Their relative amounts can vary; mixing them does not create a new fixed-ratio compound.
selfCheck: Can I explain why O₂ is an element even though it consists of molecules?
Can I distinguish a fixed ratio within a compound from variable proportions in a mixture?
transferQuestion: Liquid water and ethanol are mixed without a chemical reaction. They form one uniform liquid phase. Is the result a compound or a mixture? Explain why its uniform appearance does not decide the answer.
transferExplanation: It is a homogeneous mixture. Water and ethanol remain different substances, and their proportions can vary. A uniform appearance does not mean that a new chemical compound has formed.

title: Count particles in an aluminium ion
question: An aluminium ion is written ²⁷₁₃Al³⁺. State its numbers of protons, neutrons and electrons, and identify which particles are inside the nucleus. Explain how your electron count agrees with the ion charge.
hints: The lower number is the proton number, Z. The upper number is the nucleon number, A: protons plus neutrons.
A 3+ ion has three fewer electrons than the neutral atom. Ion formation does not change its proton or neutron numbers.
workedExplanation: The nucleus contains 13 protons and 27 − 13 = 14 neutrons.
A neutral aluminium atom has 13 electrons. The 3+ ion has lost 3, so it has 13 − 3 = 10 electrons outside the nucleus.
The 13 positive proton charges and 10 negative electron charges give a net charge of +3. Neutrons do not contribute to the charge.
selfCheck: Did I subtract proton number from nucleon number to find neutrons?
Did I change only the electron count when accounting for the positive ion charge?
transferQuestion: A neutral magnesium atom is written ²⁴₁₂Mg. How many protons, neutrons and electrons does it contain?
transferExplanation: It contains 12 protons, 24 − 12 = 12 neutrons, and 12 electrons. The proton and electron charges cancel because the atom is neutral.

title: Separate isotope identity from ion charge
question: Compare neutral ³⁵₁₇Cl and neutral ³⁷₁₇Cl. Give the proton, neutron and electron counts for each. Explain why they are isotopes of the same element rather than different elements.
hints: Element identity is determined by proton number. Both symbols have Z = 17.
For each isotope, neutrons = nucleon number − proton number. A neutral atom has equal numbers of protons and electrons.
workedExplanation: Both atoms have 17 protons and 17 electrons, so they are neutral atoms of the same element, chlorine.
Chlorine-35 has 35 − 17 = 18 neutrons. Chlorine-37 has 37 − 17 = 20 neutrons.
They are isotopes because they have the same proton number but different neutron numbers. The difference of two neutrons changes the nucleon number, not the element.
selfCheck: Can I identify what stays the same when the isotope changes?
Can I distinguish a neutron-number change from an electron-number change?
transferQuestion: The ³⁷Cl atom gains one electron to become ³⁷Cl⁻. Has it become a new isotope? State its new electron count and explain.
transferExplanation: No. It now has 18 electrons, but the nucleus still contains 17 protons and 20 neutrons. Gaining an electron changes the charge, not the isotope identity.

title: Read the brackets in a formula
question: Calculate the relative formula mass, Mᵣ, of Ca(OH)₂ using Aᵣ(Ca) = 40.1, Aᵣ(O) = 16.0 and Aᵣ(H) = 1.0. Show how many of each atom the formula represents, and state whether Mᵣ has a unit.
hints: The subscript 2 outside the brackets applies to both O and H: the formula represents one Ca, two O and two H atoms.
Add the supplied relative atomic masses for those atoms. A relative mass is a ratio, rather than a mass measured in grams.
workedExplanation: The formula represents Ca₁O₂H₂: one calcium atom and two of each atom in the hydroxide group.
Relative formula mass is dimensionless: Mᵣ = 74.1, with no unit. The molar mass of this substance would instead be expressed in g mol⁻¹; it is a different quantity.
selfCheck: Did I apply the bracket multiplier to both oxygen and hydrogen?
Did I keep the relative mass dimensionless rather than attach g or g mol⁻¹?
transferQuestion: Using the same Aᵣ values for H and O, calculate Mᵣ for H₂O and state its unit, if any.
transferExplanation: Mᵣ(H₂O) = 2 × 1.0 + 16.0 = 18.0. It is a relative mass, so it has no unit.

title: Use molar mass with its units
question: Use Aᵣ(C) = 12.0 and Aᵣ(O) = 16.0 to find the molar mass of CO₂. Then calculate the mass of 0.250 mol of CO₂. Give units at each step.
hints: One CO₂ molecule has one carbon atom and two oxygen atoms. The numerical value of its molar mass in g mol⁻¹ is 12.0 + 2 × 16.0.
Use mass = amount × molar mass, or m = nM. Check that mol × g mol⁻¹ gives grams.
workedExplanation: M(CO₂) = 12.0 + 2 × 16.0 = 44.0 g mol⁻¹. Molar mass is mass per mole, not the mass of a single molecule.
The mole units cancel, leaving grams. Here M is 44.0 g mol⁻¹; the dimensionless relative molecular mass is a different quantity with the same numerical value.
selfCheck: Did I include both oxygen atoms in the molar mass?
Can I explain why the final answer is in g rather than mol or g mol⁻¹?
transferQuestion: What amount of CO₂ is present in a 22.0 g sample, using M(CO₂) = 44.0 g mol⁻¹?
transferExplanation: n = m/M = 22.0 g ÷ 44.0 g mol⁻¹ = 0.500 mol. Dividing mass by mass per mole leaves an amount in moles.

title: Explain the signs of ion charges
question: A neutral magnesium atom has 12 electrons and a neutral oxygen atom has 8. In a simple ion-formation model, magnesium loses two electrons and oxygen gains two. Write the resulting ions, state their electron counts, and explain the charge signs without changing the nuclei.
hints: Electrons carry negative charge. Losing them leaves an excess of positive charge; gaining them leaves an excess of negative charge.
Magnesium keeps 12 protons and oxygen keeps 8 protons. Compare those counts with the new electron counts.
workedExplanation: Magnesium forms Mg²⁺, a cation, with 12 − 2 = 10 electrons. Its 12 positive proton charges exceed the 10 negative electron charges by two.
Oxygen forms O²⁻, an anion, with 8 + 2 = 10 electrons. Its 10 negative electron charges exceed the 8 positive proton charges by two.
Only electrons are lost or gained in this model. Neither nucleus changes, so the elements remain magnesium and oxygen.
selfCheck: Did I connect electron loss to a positive charge and electron gain to a negative charge?
Did I keep proton numbers unchanged while counting the new electrons?
transferQuestion: A neutral sodium atom has 11 electrons. It loses one electron. Write the ion and give its electron count.
transferExplanation: It forms Na⁺ with 10 electrons. The nucleus still contains 11 protons, giving one more positive charge than negative charge.

title: Explain what holds a covalent bond together
question: Two hydrogen atoms form H₂ by sharing a pair of electrons. Explain the electrostatic attraction that holds the atoms together. Why would saying that the two electrons attract each other be incorrect? Does each hydrogen need an octet?
hints: Identify the signs of the charges: nuclei are positive and electrons are negative.
The shared pair is attracted to both nuclei. The first electron shell can hold only two electrons, so hydrogen is an exception to an octet description.
workedExplanation: The negatively charged shared electron pair is attracted to both positively charged hydrogen nuclei. This electron–nucleus attraction is the basis of the covalent bond.

The electrons repel each other; they do not provide an electron–electron attraction. Nuclei also repel each other. The stable bond distance reflects the balance of attractive and repulsive interactions.
Each hydrogen shares access to two electrons in its first shell. Hydrogen has a filled first shell with two electrons, not an octet; the octet rule is a tendency with exceptions.
selfCheck: Can I name both the negative and positive charges involved in the bonding attraction?
Can I explain why a shared pair does not mean that two electrons attract each other?
Did I avoid applying an eight-electron shell requirement to hydrogen?
transferQuestion: In a simple Lewis representation, each chlorine atom in Cl₂ has three lone pairs and the atoms share one bonding pair. How many valence-shell electrons are counted around each chlorine, and which charges provide the bond attraction?
transferExplanation: Each chlorine counts 6 electrons in its three lone pairs and 2 in the shared pair, giving 8 valence-shell electrons. The shared negative electron pair is attracted to both positive nuclei; the electrons do not attract each other.

title: Use shape as well as bond polarity
question: CO₂ is linear, with two equal polar C=O bonds at 180°. H₂O is bent, with two equal polar O–H bonds at about 104.5°. Predict whether each molecule is polar and explain using the directions of the bond dipoles. Treat each molecule as an isolated molecule in this simple model.
hints: A molecule can contain polar bonds without having a net molecular dipole. Consider the bond dipoles as vectors.
In linear CO₂ the equal dipoles point in opposite directions. In bent H₂O they are not opposite, so ask whether their vector sum is zero.
workedExplanation: In CO₂ the two equal C=O bond dipoles point toward the oxygen atoms in opposite directions. Their vector sum is zero, so this linear molecule is non-polar in the model.
In H₂O the O–H bond dipoles both point toward oxygen, but the molecule is bent. The dipoles do not cancel, giving a net molecular dipole; water is polar.
Bond polarity alone is insufficient: the molecular geometry determines whether the individual bond dipoles cancel.
selfCheck: Did I use both bond polarity and molecular shape?
Can I explain why polar bonds do not necessarily make a polar molecule?
transferQuestion: BF₃ is trigonal planar, with three identical polar B–F bonds arranged at 120° in one plane. Predict its molecular polarity in the same simple isolated-molecule model and justify the answer.
transferExplanation: The three equal bond-dipole vectors point toward the fluorine atoms and cancel by symmetry. Ideal trigonal planar BF₃ is non-polar despite having polar bonds.

title: State which entities you are counting
question: A sample contains 0.500 mol of CO₂. Calculate the number of CO₂ molecules and the number of oxygen atoms in the sample. Use Nₐ = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹, rounded here from the exact Avogadro constant. State the type of entity alongside each answer.
hints: Use number of entities = amount × Avogadro constant, or N = nNₐ. The amount given refers to CO₂ molecules, not oxygen atoms.
Each CO₂ molecule contains two oxygen atoms. Multiply the molecule count by two to count oxygen atoms.
workedExplanation: N(CO₂ molecules) = 0.500 mol × 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹ = 3.01 × 10²³ CO₂ molecules. The mol units cancel, leaving a count of specified entities.
There are two oxygen atoms per CO₂ molecule, so the oxygen-atom count is 2 × 3.01 × 10²³ = 6.02 × 10²³ oxygen atoms.
The mole measures amount of substance, not mass. Naming the entity matters: this sample has 0.500 mol of CO₂ molecules but 1.00 mol of oxygen atoms.
selfCheck: Did I label my counts as molecules or atoms rather than simply write particles?
Did I use two oxygen atoms per CO₂ molecule without changing the number of molecules?
transferQuestion: Using the same rounded Nₐ, how many NaCl formula units are represented by 0.100 mol of solid sodium chloride? Explain why formula units is a more appropriate label than NaCl molecules.
transferExplanation: N = 0.100 mol × 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹ = 6.02 × 10²² NaCl formula units. Solid sodium chloride is an extended ionic lattice, not a collection of discrete NaCl molecules; the formula unit specifies its simplest ion ratio.

title: Turn an atom ratio into a molecular formula
question: A molecular compound contains only carbon and hydrogen. A sample contains 4.80 g of carbon and 0.800 g of hydrogen, and the compound's independently measured molar mass is 56.0 g mol⁻¹. Use Aᵣ(C) = 12.0 and Aᵣ(H) = 1.00 to determine its empirical formula and molecular formula. Show why the mass ratio is not the atom ratio.
hints: Convert each element's mass to an amount in moles. Equal amounts of atoms contain equal numbers of atoms, so the mole ratio gives the atom ratio.
Divide both amounts by the smaller amount for the simplest whole-number ratio. Then compare the molar mass with the mass of one mole of empirical-formula units.
workedExplanation: n(C) = 4.80 g ÷ 12.0 g mol⁻¹ = 0.400 mol, and n(H) = 0.800 g ÷ 1.00 g mol⁻¹ = 0.800 mol. Carbon atoms are heavier than hydrogen atoms, so the mass ratio alone does not give their number ratio.
Divide both amounts by 0.400 mol: C:H = 1:2. The simplest whole-number atom ratio is therefore CH₂, the empirical formula.
One mole of CH₂ empirical-formula units has a mass of 12.0 + 2 × 1.00 = 14.0 g. The molecular molar mass is four times this value: 56.0 ÷ 14.0 = 4.
Multiply both empirical subscripts by four to obtain C₄H₈. The molecular formula specifies four carbon atoms and eight hydrogen atoms per molecule; CH₂ specifies only their simplest ratio.
selfCheck: Did I compare amounts in moles rather than reduce the original mass ratio?
Did I multiply every empirical subscript by the same whole number and check the resulting molar mass?
transferQuestion: A different molecular compound has empirical formula CH₂ and molar mass 42.0 g mol⁻¹. Using the same relative atomic masses, find its molecular formula.
transferExplanation: One mole of CH₂ empirical-formula units has a mass of 14.0 g. The multiplier is 42.0 ÷ 14.0 = 3, so the molecular formula is C₃H₆, with both subscripts multiplied by three.

title: Distinguish ion formation from the ionic bond
question: A sodium chloride crystal contains Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions. A student says, 'The ionic bond is the electron being transferred, and each Na⁺ attracts only the Cl⁻ that received its electron.' Correct both parts using electrostatic interactions. Also state the interaction between two Na⁺ ions.
hints: Opposite charges attract and like charges repel. Identify the charges present after the ions have formed.
An ion's electrostatic attraction is not restricted to one partner by the history of an electron. Consider neighbouring ions throughout a three-dimensional crystal.
workedExplanation: The ionic bond is the electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions: positive Na⁺ ions attract negative Cl⁻ ions. Electron transfer can explain ion formation, but the transfer event itself is not the bond.

Each Na⁺ can attract surrounding Cl⁻ ions in different directions; the attraction is not limited to a particular ion that received an electron. The crystal is an extended arrangement of ions rather than independent bonded pairs.
Two Na⁺ ions repel because they have like charges. Both attractions and repulsions matter in a stable lattice; it would be incorrect to say that all neighbouring charges attract.
selfCheck: Did I describe an attraction between ions, rather than call electron transfer the bond?
Can I explain why opposite charges attract, like charges repel, and the attraction is not restricted to one named partner?
transferQuestion: Magnesium oxide contains Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ ions. Which pair attracts, Mg²⁺ with O²⁻ or Mg²⁺ with Mg²⁺? Does the definition of the ionic bond change because the charges have magnitude two?
transferExplanation: Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ attract because their charges are opposite; two Mg²⁺ ions repel. The definition remains electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions. A charge of magnitude two does not make electron transfer itself the bond.

title: Read an ionic formula as a lattice ratio
question: Solid magnesium chloride contains Mg²⁺ and Cl⁻ ions in a three-dimensional repeating lattice. Find the simplest ion-number ratio that gives zero net charge and write the empirical formula. Explain why this formula should not be read as a collection of isolated molecules in the crystal.
hints: One Mg²⁺ contributes +2. How many Cl⁻ ions, each contributing −1, are needed to balance that charge?
The subscripts describe the simplest ratio in the extended structure. They do not mark the boundary of a separate molecule.
workedExplanation: One Mg²⁺ and two Cl⁻ give a total charge of +2 + 2 × (−1) = 0. The simplest Mg²⁺:Cl⁻ ion-number ratio is 1:2.

The empirical formula is MgCl₂. The subscript 2 records twice as many chloride ions as magnesium ions; it does not mean that magnesium has a charge of +1 or that chlorine atoms are paired as Cl₂ molecules.

The solid is a three-dimensional lattice extending through many ions, not isolated MgCl₂ molecules. A formula unit is a way of expressing the simplest composition ratio, rather than a discrete particle cut out of the crystal.
selfCheck: Does my simplest ratio balance the total positive and negative charges?
Can I distinguish a formula unit in an extended ionic lattice from a separate molecule?
transferQuestion: An aluminium oxide lattice contains Al³⁺ and O²⁻ ions. Find the simplest neutral ion-number ratio and its empirical formula.
transferExplanation: The smallest matching total charge is six: two Al³⁺ contribute +6 and three O²⁻ contribute −6. The simplest Al³⁺:O²⁻ ratio is 2:3, so the empirical formula is Al₂O₃, not a formula for isolated molecules in the solid.

title: Separate electron domains from molecular shape
question: In CH₄ the central carbon has four bonding pairs and no lone pairs. In NH₃ the central nitrogen has three bonding pairs and one lone pair. Count each single bond and each lone pair as one electron domain. Use VSEPR to predict the electron-domain arrangement and molecular shape of each. Use 109.5° as the ideal tetrahedral reference and explain qualitatively how the lone pair affects the H–N–H angle; no exact ammonia angle is required.
hints: Four electron domains arrange approximately tetrahedrally to reduce repulsion. Count lone pairs as well as bonds when finding the domain arrangement.
The molecular shape describes the positions of atoms, not the lone pair. Lone-pair repulsion can compress the angles between bonding domains.
workedExplanation: CH₄ has four electron domains, all bonding. Its electron-domain arrangement and molecular shape are both tetrahedral, with ideal H–C–H angles of 109.5°.

NH₃ also has four electron domains: three bonding and one lone pair. Its electron-domain arrangement is approximately tetrahedral, but the three hydrogen positions give a trigonal pyramidal molecular shape.

The lone pair occupies one domain and repels the bonding domains more strongly than they repel one another in this model. The H–N–H angle is therefore somewhat smaller than 109.5°. A domain arrangement is not automatically the molecular shape.
selfCheck: Did I count the lone pair when finding the number of electron domains?
Did I name the shape using atom positions and distinguish it from the electron-domain arrangement?
transferQuestion: In H₂O the central oxygen has two bonding pairs and two lone pairs. Predict its electron-domain arrangement and molecular shape using the same model. Should two bonded atoms alone make it linear?
transferExplanation: There are four electron domains, so the electron-domain arrangement is approximately tetrahedral. The two hydrogen positions give a bent molecular shape, not a linear one. The two lone pairs must be included in the domain count, even though they are not atom positions.

title: Use electronegativity to locate partial charges
question: Use the supplied electronegativities C = 2.6, O = 3.4 and F = 4.0. Compare the polarity of a C–O bond with a C–F bond in a simple shared-electron model. Calculate each electronegativity difference, identify the partial charges, and decide whether an F–F bond is polar. These are bond comparisons, not predictions of whole-molecule polarity.
hints: Electronegativity describes an atom's attraction for shared electrons. The more electronegative atom in a polar bond is partially negative.
Subtract the smaller electronegativity from the larger. A larger difference indicates a more polar bond in this model; equal values give no bond dipole.
workedExplanation: For C–O, the electronegativity difference is 3.4 − 2.6 = 0.8. Oxygen attracts the shared electrons more strongly, so the partial charges are Cδ⁺–Oδ⁻.
For C–F, the difference is 4.0 − 2.6 = 1.4. The partial charges are Cδ⁺–Fδ⁻. Its larger electronegativity difference makes C–F more polar than C–O in this model.

For F–F, the difference is 4.0 − 4.0 = 0.0. Equal atoms share the bonding electrons equally, so this bond is non-polar. The δ symbols describe partial charges in covalent bonds, not full ionic charges.
selfCheck: Did I place δ⁻ on the more electronegative atom and δ⁺ on the other atom?
Did I compare electronegativity differences without treating partial charges as full ion charges or inferring an entire molecule's polarity?
transferQuestion: Given H = 2.2 and Cl = 3.2 on the same electronegativity scale, calculate the H–Cl bond's electronegativity difference and identify its partial charges.
transferExplanation: The difference is 3.2 − 2.2 = 1.0. Chlorine attracts the shared electrons more strongly, giving Hδ⁺–Clδ⁻. These partial charges do not mean that the molecule consists of a free H⁺ ion and a free Cl⁻ ion.

title: Identify attractions between particles
question: Consider separate pure samples of CH₄, HCl and NH₃. CH₄ is non-polar; HCl and NH₃ are polar. Only NH₃ has H directly bonded to N, O or F. Identify the intermolecular attractions in each sample in the usual introductory model. Then describe the additional attraction when a polar HCl molecule approaches an Ar atom with no permanent dipole. Distinguish these attractions from covalent bonds within molecules.
hints: London (dispersion) forces occur between all these neutral particles. Polar molecules also have permanent dipoles, which can attract other permanent dipoles or induce a dipole in a neighbouring particle.
Hydrogen bonding requires H directly bonded to N, O or F interacting with a suitable lone pair on a neighbouring particle. Simply containing hydrogen is insufficient.
workedExplanation: All three pure samples have London (dispersion) forces arising from temporary fluctuations in electron distributions. For non-polar CH₄, these are the only intermolecular attractions in this model.
Pure HCl also has dipole–dipole attractions between its permanent molecular dipoles. It does not have hydrogen bonding in this model because its H is bonded to Cl rather than N, O or F.
Pure NH₃ has London forces, dipole–dipole attractions and hydrogen bonding. An N–H hydrogen on one molecule can interact with the nitrogen lone pair on another molecule.

An approaching HCl molecule can distort the Ar electron cloud and induce a dipole. Attraction between the permanent HCl dipole and the induced Ar dipole is dipole-induced dipole attraction; London forces also operate between these particles.
These attractions act between particles. They are distinct from the covalent C–H, H–Cl and N–H bonds within the molecules.
selfCheck: Did I include London forces even for polar and hydrogen-bonding molecules?
Did I check what atom H is bonded to, rather than assume every hydrogen-containing molecule forms hydrogen bonds?
Can I distinguish a permanent dipole from a dipole induced in a neighbouring particle?
transferQuestion: Pure CH₃F consists of polar molecules, but all three H atoms are bonded to carbon. Do the molecules form hydrogen bonds with one another in this model? State the intermolecular attractions that still occur.
transferExplanation: Pure CH₃F does not form hydrogen bonds with itself in this model: it has no H directly bonded to N, O or F. It still has London forces and dipole–dipole attractions. Having a fluorine atom somewhere in the formula is insufficient for self hydrogen bonding.

title: Compare intermolecular forces under stated conditions
question: Compare C₂H₆ (molar mass 30 g mol⁻¹, non-polar), CH₃F (34 g mol⁻¹, polar, with every H bonded to C), and CH₃OH (32 g mol⁻¹, polar, with an O–H group). Their molar masses are comparable. At the same external pressure, use the introductory intermolecular-force model to predict the order of boiling temperatures from lowest to highest. Explain why boiling does not require breaking the covalent O–H bond.
hints: All three have London forces. Identify which sample also has permanent dipole–dipole attractions and which can form hydrogen bonds between its own molecules.

For comparable molar masses, stronger intermolecular attractions generally require more energy to separate molecules. Keep that condition in your comparison rather than turn the force ranking into a universal rule.
workedExplanation: C₂H₆ has London forces only in this model. CH₃F also has dipole–dipole attractions, but its C–H bonds do not provide hydrogen-bond donors. CH₃OH can form hydrogen bonds through its O–H group and the oxygen lone pairs; it also has London and dipole–dipole attractions.

With these comparable molar masses, the expected order is C₂H₆ < CH₃F < CH₃OH for boiling temperature at the same external pressure. The general relative-force comparison is London < dipole–dipole < hydrogen bonding under this condition.
Boiling separates molecules against intermolecular attractions. The molecules retain their covalent bonds; it does not require breaking the O–H covalent bond within methanol.

This is a conditional trend, not a universal ranking of every substance. Electron-cloud size, polarizability and molecular shape can change London attractions; the force label alone is insufficient when comparing very different molecules.
selfCheck: Did I state that the molar masses are comparable and the external pressure is the same?
Did I compare attractions between molecules, include London forces for all samples, and keep covalent bonds distinct from those attractions?
transferQuestion: A student claims, 'Every hydrogen-bonding substance must boil above every non-polar substance.' Does this example justify that claim? Identify the missing condition without guessing an unknown boiling temperature.
transferExplanation: No. The general ranking used here assumes comparable molar masses. Larger, more polarizable non-polar molecules can have strong London attractions, and molecular shape also matters. You cannot infer a universal boiling-temperature order from the name of one force alone.
